subject: science
passage: In the early 1900s, only a few dozen greater one-horned rhinoceroses may have survived in the area that is now Kaziranga National Park in northeastern India. Today the park holds more than 2,000 of them. Wildlife officials usually credit this recovery to strict protection: armed guards patrol the park, and hunting rhinos for their horns is severely punished.
passage_b: Protection from poachers has clearly been essential, but ecologist Rupa Bordoloi argues that it tells only part of the story. Every year, the Brahmaputra River floods much of Kaziranga, leaving fresh silt that renews the tall grasslands rhinos depend on for food. Without these floods, she notes, the grasslands would slowly turn into woodland that could support far fewer rhinos.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation offered by wildlife officials in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting that protection mattered while arguing that yearly floods also helped
choices.B: By arguing that the floods, not protection from hunters, explain the recovery
choices.C: By questioning whether the number of rhinos in the park has truly increased
choices.D: By suggesting that the floods threaten rhinos by destroying their grasslands

explanation.why: Text 1 credits the rhinos' recovery to "strict protection." Text 2 calls protection "clearly... essential" but says it "tells only part of the story," because the Brahmaputra's floods renew the grasslands rhinos feed on. So the author of Text 2 would accept the officials' explanation as incomplete and add the role of flooding.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 agrees that protection was essential and adds that floods keep the rhinos' grasslands from turning into woodland.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 calls protection "essential"; it adds floods as another factor rather than replacing protection with them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 does not question the population figures in Text 1.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the floods renew the grasslands, the opposite of destroying them.
